title: Accounting: the language of finance
hook: A public company has to publish its books for everyone to read. Why would it, and what do you look for once it does?
objectives: Explain why public companies publish standardized, audited statements, and where that system still depends on you.
Tell the balance sheet, income statement and cash flow statement apart, and say why income is not cash.
Use Assets = Liabilities + Equity and net working capital to read a balance sheet.

steps.title: Course map: why accounting comes first

blocks.md:
The course runs in parts: accounting basics, then time value of money and NPV, then bonds, then valuation and capital budgeting, then portfolio theory after the midterm.

> "Accounting is the language of finance."

You cannot value Microsoft without forecasting its cash flows, and the forecast starts from its accounting history: revenues, costs, profits, capital spending.

blocks.q: Why does a valuation course begin with accounting?
options: Forecasts of future cash flow are built from past accounting numbers
Exams are mostly accounting problems, so the course front-loads them as practice
The textbook happens to start with accounting, so the lectures follow its order
Auditors require every investor to learn accounting before they may buy stock
blocks.why: The professor's point: nobody knows the future, so you project it from the revenues, costs and capital spending in the accounting record.

steps.title: Why companies must publish their books

blocks.md:
US public companies file annual and quarterly reports in a standard format (GAAP), checked by outside auditors. The goal is *apples to apples*: everyone sees the same data, so whoever makes the most of it earns the reward.

Auditors remove the CEO's conflict of interest. But:

> "Who audits the auditors?" ... "So ultimately it's you."

blocks.title: How trust in the numbers is built

frames.title: Publish everything
frames.text: If some investors had more information than others, society could not tell who deserves the capital. So everyone gets the same reports.

frames.title: Standardize it
frames.text: GAAP means two companies reporting profit are talking about the same thing. Accounting is complicated enough without every firm inventing its own rules.

frames.title: Audit it
frames.text: A third party checks the statements, because the CEO and CFO have a conflict of interest. This creates confidence in the data.

frames.title: Stay skeptical
frames.text: Nobody audits the auditors beyond regulators and the market. Some statements are too good to be true, and the responsibility lands on the investor.

blocks.headline: SEC Still Pursuing Accounting Fraud
blocks.tieIn: The article describes an SEC complaint against three former AMMO, Inc. executives alleging a years-long scheme to mislead investors and falsify corporate records, including changing how Adjusted EBITDA was calculated to show false profitability. These are allegations, not findings. It is the professor's warning in practice: standardized, audited statements still need a skeptical reader.

blocks.q: What does requiring GAAP statements achieve for investors?
options: Reported profits can be compared like for like
Every public company reports exactly the same profit number
Investors no longer need to read the statements at all
Auditors guarantee that fraud can never occur
blocks.why: Standardizing means profit at one firm and profit at another are defined the same way. It does not make the numbers identical or fraud-proof.

blocks.md:
All three describe the same company. The **balance sheet** is what you have: assets and liabilities. The **income statement** is the profit over a period. The **statement of cash flows** tracks cash moving in and out.

> "They are not the same thing."

That is why value is the discounted value of future *cash flow*, not of future income.

blocks.prompt: Which statement would you find each item on?

items.label: Cash and marketable securities on hand today
Cash paid out to buy new equipment
Money owed to suppliers and banks
How much cash the firm generated over 12 months

targets: Cash flow statement (cash in and out)
blocks.why: Balance sheet items are measured at one date. Income and cash flow statements cover a stretch of time, but income is an accounting profit while cash flow is actual cash.

blocks.text: "You can have income without cash flow or even negative cash flow." Cash is what you pay at the store. You do not pay in profits.

blocks.q: A customer buys $5,000 of product on credit and will pay next month. What does this year's picture show?
options: Revenue and cash both rise by $5,000 right away
Revenue counts, but no cash yet
Neither changes until the customer actually pays
Cash rises, but revenue is not counted yet
blocks.why: Income is an accounting concept, so the sale counts as revenue. The cash arrives later, which is why the two statements differ.

blocks.md:
Every balance sheet obeys one rule: **Assets = Liabilities + Equity**. Equity is what is left for the owners after the debts.

Borrowing a billion dollars to build a data center changes nothing about equity on day one. The professor's point is what happens if the NPV was positive: over time the assets outgrow the liabilities.

frames.title: Before
frames.text: A firm owns $10B of assets and owes $4B. The owners' equity is the gap.

frames.title: Borrow and build
frames.text: Take a $1B loan and spend it on the data center. Both sides grow by the same amount. Nothing has been created yet.

frames.title: The NPV pays off
frames.text: If the analysis was right, the data center's future cash flows make the firm's assets worth more than the debt used to build them. Say assets reach $11.3B.

frames.title: Read the result
frames.text: Equity grew by the value created. Hopefully you see that growth year after year.

blocks.title: Equity is what is left
blocks.caption: Slide liabilities above assets and equity goes negative.

steps.title: Current vs long-term, and net working capital

blocks.md:
"Current" means within 12 months. It matters because current assets let you survive: if you cannot cover salaries and rent, you go out of business. Cash is the obvious one, but you need *something pretty close to cash*, like marketable securities.

**Net working capital** = current assets minus current liabilities. It shows how ready you are for an emergency.

rows.label: Assets
cells: Cash, marketable securities, accounts receivable, inventory

rows.label: Liabilities
cells: Short-term debt, bills owed to suppliers, wages, taxes, debt coming due
Long-term debt, equipment leases, deferred taxes

rows.label: Why you care
cells: Decides whether you survive the next year
Capacity for the long run, and depreciation

blocks.title: Lemonade stand: how ready are you?
blocks.caption: Default: $20k cash + $50k stock + $5k receivables + $15k inventory = $90k, against $60k due soon.

blocks.q: On inventory, what does the professor say about six years' supply versus six days' supply?
options: Six years is bad and six days is fine
Both extremes are risky, and a balance is needed
Six years is fine and six days is bad
Neither tells you anything
blocks.why: Six years ties up cash in stock that is not selling. Six days risks running out. You want a balance for your industry.

steps.title: Depreciation: income that is not cash

blocks.md:
Long-term assets wear out on paper. Residential real estate is depreciated over 27.5 years, so a $275,000 structure writes off $10,000 a year.

Own a rental that nets $10,000 in cash. On the accounting statement, the $10,000 depreciation cancels it, so taxable income is zero. Cash flow and income disagree, and neither is wrong.

blocks.title: The same rental, two measures ($ per year)
blocks.caption: $275,000 / 27.5 years = $10,000 of depreciation, which uses no cash.

blocks.q: A $550,000 building is depreciated over 27.5 years. What does each year's depreciation do?
options: Uses $20,000 of cash
Adds $20,000 of cash
Lowers income by $20,000 but uses no cash
Raises income by $20,000
blocks.why: 550,000 / 27.5 = 20,000. It reduces accounting income (and the tax bill) without any cash leaving.

recap: Public companies publish standardized, audited statements so investors compare apples to apples. Nobody audits the auditors, so skepticism is yours.
Balance sheet = what you have (Assets = Liabilities + Equity). Income statement = profit. Cash flow statement = cash. Income is not cash.
Current items come due within 12 months. Net working capital = current assets - current liabilities, a readiness check.
Depreciation lowers accounting income and taxes but uses no cash.

quiz.q: The main reason public companies must publish standardized statements is to
options: let investors compare companies
make sure every firm reports the same profit
keep the CEO from ever seeing the numbers
give auditors a reason to exist
quiz.why: Standardized, public data lets whoever analyzes it best earn the reward, which steers capital to good firms.

quiz.q: Which statement is a snapshot of the firm at a single date?
options: Income statement
Statement of cash flows
Balance sheet
Both income and cash flow statements
quiz.why: The balance sheet shows assets and liabilities at one point in time. The other two cover a period.

quiz.q: A firm has $80M of assets and $55M of liabilities. What is its book equity?
Current assets are $150k and current liabilities are $180k. What does net working capital tell you?
options: It is +$30k, so the firm is comfortable
It is -$30k, so the firm may struggle with near-term bills
It is $330k, the firm's total size
It is zero, so the firm breaks even
quiz.why: 150 - 180 = -30. Negative working capital means short-term obligations exceed short-term assets.

quiz.q: Why is value defined from future cash flow rather than future income?
options: Cash flow is always larger than income
Income is never positive for real companies
Income is an accounting concept, and you can have income without cash
Taxes are not charged on cash
quiz.why: Income depends on accounting choices like depreciation and credit sales. Cash flow is the actual money.

flashcards.back: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles. Standard rules so statements from different companies are comparable (apples to apples).

flashcards.front: Why auditors, and who audits them?
flashcards.back: Third-party auditors remove the CEO/CFO conflict of interest and create confidence. Nobody fully audits the auditors, so the investor must stay skeptical.
Balance sheet (assets and liabilities, a snapshot), income statement (profit over a period), statement of cash flows (cash in and out).
Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Equity (book value) = Assets - Liabilities, and it can be negative.
Current assets - current liabilities. A readiness check: how prepared you are for near-term bills or an emergency.
Income is an accounting profit. Cash flow is cash. Depreciation and credit sales are two reasons they differ.
